newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House tax panel considers tax cut legislation.
newsitem.headline: U.S. House tax panel considers tax cut legislation.

text.p: The House tax-writing committee began consideration Wednesday of legislation to cut taxes by a net $85 billion over five years with Republicans and Democrats at odds over key provisions.

The House Ways and Means Committee started work on a proposal from Chairman Bill Archer, a Texas Republican, of how to accomplish the amount of tax cuts agreed to in a budget pact between congressional Republicans and the White House.
Democrats and the White House attacked the tax plan, saying it favoured wealthier Americans over the poor. Archer says the plan gives the most benefit to the middle class.
"Clearly this is not everything the president would want, we have made significant progress. It's not everything I want," Archer said at the start of the meeting.
All tax legislation must originate in the House Ways and Means committee and consideration of the bill was expected to go late into the night and start again on Thursday.
Archer's legislation included tax incentives for higher education, a child tax credit and a reduction in the capital gains tax.
There was some last-minute tinkering by Archer to his provisions on inheritance tax relief and extending the airline ticket tax.

The estate tax change would gradually increase the threshold where estate taxes kick in to $1 million in 2007 from the current $600,000. Previously in Archer's bill that $1 million mark would have been reached in 2014.
That change would more than double the cost of the estate tax relief to $7.5 billion over five years from the previous $3.1 billion.
That increase would be paid for by reducing the cost of the corporate alternative minimum tax proposal. Under the change, that tax would be repealed only for small businesses, not large corporations.
Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said he was "gratified" by Republican plans to modify the alternative minimum tax phase-out proposal, but questioned using the money to offer more estate tax relief.

Another change in Archer's bill would earmark funds from a 4.3 cents-per-gallon tax on aviation gasoline and jet fuel for the Airport and Airway Trust Fund that pays for airport repairs and improvements. Initially the money from that tax would have been put in the general fund.
The revised Archer bill would also not apply domestic air transportation taxes to the domestic leg of an international flight as previously proposed.

House Democrats planned to offer an alternative tax bill in the committee that would provide $37 billion over five years for higher education tax credits and $71 billion for a phased-in $500 per child tax credit for children under age 18. Archer's child tax credit would cover children under age 17.
The Democratic plan would provide a more targeted capital gains tax cut than Archer's plan, focusing on small businesses, family farms and real estate.

Representative Jim Nussle, an Iowa Republican, planned to introduce an amendment to strip ethanol language from the tax package. Archer has proposed paring down the tax break supporting production of the corn-based fuel and eliminating it in 2000.

The proposal to reduce the ethanol subsidy raised opposition from lawmakers from farm states and agriculture groups. House Speaker Newt Gingrich, a Georgia Republican, has previously questioned whether there was currently enough support to eliminate the ethanol subsidy.
Representative Nancy Johnson, a Connecticut Republican, said she planned to offer an amendment to increase the cigarette tax to 53 cents a pack from 24 cents to fund children's health insurance.
